title: Suspected primary CNS vasculitis
consultQuestion: Multifocal strokes or abnormal angiogram — is this CNS vasculitis or a mimic like RCVS?
keyHistory: Subacute headache, cognitive decline, focal deficits, seizures over weeks–months
Systemic symptoms, rash, oral ulcers, sicca (secondary vasculitis)
Immunosuppression, HIV, syphilis risk, TB exposure
keyExam: Skin, joints, eyes for systemic disease
redFlags: Normal brain MRI — PACNS very unlikely
Thunderclap onset, normal parenchyma, convexity SAH — favors RCVS (avoid steroids)

clues: Subacute course, multifocal infarcts, inflammatory CSF, enhancing lesions
Thunderclap, triggers, normal MRI or cSAH, minimal vessel-wall enhancement
Eccentric plaque on vessel-wall MRI, vascular risk

differential.dx: Infectious vasculitis (VZV, syphilis, TB, fungal, HIV, endocarditis)
clues: Recent zoster, CSF anti-VZV IgG, serologies

differential.dx: Secondary CNS vasculitis (connective tissue disease, systemic vasculitis, Behçet)

clues: Vasogenic edema, leptomeningeal enhancement, lobar microbleeds

differential.dx: Moyamoya, FMD, radiation vasculopathy, APS, MOGAD, CADASIL

workup.test: MRI brain with and without gadolinium, DWI, SWI
notes: Normal MRI makes CNS vasculitis very unlikely
Concentric smooth enhancement favors vasculitis over plaque or RCVS; specificity not established
Less sensitive for medium-sized and posterior-circulation vessels

workup.test: LP: cells, protein, glucose, Gram stain/culture, VZV PCR and CSF anti-VZV IgG, syphilis, fungal studies, cytology, flow cytometry
notes: Inflammatory CSF in ~75%; mainly used to rule out mimics

workup.test: Serum: ESR, CRP, ANA, ANCA, antiphospholipid antibodies, HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B/C
Brain and leptomeningeal biopsy (lesional preferred; nondominant frontal if random)
indication: Small-vessel vasculitis suspected with normal angiogram
notes: 30–50% false negatives; finds another diagnosis in ~30%

decisionRules.recommendation: 1988 Calabrese–Mallek criteria (angiographic or histological vasculitis + exclusion of other causes) — not prospectively validated

evidenceNote: ESO guideline as cited in Salvarani 2024

decisionRules.condition: Suspected small-vessel vasculitis with normal angiogram
evidenceNote: ESO guideline as cited in Salvarani 2024

decisionRules.condition: Angiography highly suggestive of medium-to-large-vessel vasculitis
decisionRules.recommendation: Biopsy only to rule out other diagnoses
evidenceNote: ESO guideline as cited in Salvarani 2024

decisionRules.recommendation: Score with RCVS2 before labeling vasculitis — see thunderclap-headache

initialSteps: Confirmed PACNS: glucocorticoids ± cyclophosphamide (Salvarani 2024) — rheumatology co-management
Hold steroids if RCVS remains likely
recsTemplate: MRI brain with contrast, DWI, SWI; vessel-wall MRI
CTA/MRA head; DSA if normal and suspicion high
LP: cells, protein, cultures, VZV PCR + CSF VZV IgG, VDRL, fungal studies, cytology/flow
ESR, CRP, ANA, ANCA, APLA, HIV, RPR, hepatitis B/C
Neurosurgery for brain/leptomeningeal biopsy [if small-vessel suspected or diagnosis uncertain]
pearls: Only 11.9% of patients with both studies had classic angiography plus pathologically confirmed vasculitis (Salvarani 2024)
Common presentations: focal deficits (67–83%), headache (54–63%), cognitive impairment (35–50%) (Salvarani 2024)
Most drug-induced 'vasculitis' on angiography is vasospasm (Salvarani 2024)
sources: Salvarani C, Brown RD Jr, Hunder GG. Primary Central Nervous System Vasculitis. N Engl J Med 2024;391:1028-1037. doi:10.1161/STR.0000000000000422
